segments.text: A Hierarchical Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning Framework for Privacy-Preserved and Low-Latency Cybersecurity in Cloud-Based Telemedicine Systems Abstract-With the simultaneous explosion of connected medical devices, and increasing real-time patient monitoring capabilities, telemedicine infrastructures have witnessed a tremendous surge in demand for intelligent, adaptive, and privacy-preserving cybersecurity mechanisms‌. In fact, most of the currently available centralized Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) frameworks, that provides high detection accuracy, have high latency, scalability problem and less explainability. This paper proposes a new hybrid architecture HIER-MA-DRL (Hierarchical Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning) to overcome those limitations to facilitate distributed threat detection for edge/cloud environments. The proposed model maintains a balance between quick response for immediate anomalies and global situational observance by integrating lightweight edge agents but also using a centralized DRL coordinator for policy optimization over long-horizons. Moreover, embedded explainable policy distillation mechanisms to guarantee transparency and faithfulness in response to automation. We conduct extensive experimental evaluation using network intrusion benchmark datasets and real-time telemedicine traffic and demonstrate that HIER-MA-DRL achieves a detection accuracy of 99.03%, a response latency of 41.8% lower, and a false positive rate of 36.5% lower than that of the conventional centralized DRL frameworks. We ensure scalability with high data stream volumes due to our hierarchical coordination between agents and we protect patient data privacy using on-device anonymization. In summary, HIER-MA-DRL provides a strong, explainable, and low-latency cybersecurity framework that can be applied to next-generation smart healthcare and telemedicine environments. Keywords-Hierarchical Multi-Agent DRL, Edge Computing, Cybersecurity, Telemedicine, Privacy Preservation, Explainable Reinforcement Learning, Low-Latency Detection, Cloud–Edge Architecture I Introduction Telemedicine and real-time patient monitoring have extremely changed the way healthcare is delivered, introducing a level of interconnectivity among medical devices, cloud and edge nodes on a level we have not seen before. On the other hand, the fast digitalization has enlarged the attack surface of health-care infrastructures and the need for intelligent cyber-security methods that can accommodate privacy concerns [1], [2]. Centralized security won't work because of latencies introduced processing high queued medical traffic, a common occurrence in tele-health applications [3][4], and doesn't also scale. While the combination of distributed learning paradigms and cloud–edge orchestration is an interesting direction to explore, upholding the desired level of speed in anomaly detection with compliance under confidentiality policies for highly sensitive patient environments are Current models may be robust and system-aware [5], but these do not consider hierarchical
segments.label: human

segments.text: mechanisms trading localized decision-making versus global optimisation. As a result, this creates an increasing demand for multi-layer, explainable, and compliant privacy-preserving learning systems able to meet the latency–security trade-off in cloud-based telemedicine environment [6]. Multi-agent reinforcement learning has also been applied as a disruptive adaptive cybersecurity and intelligent network control technology in the rapidly changing digital healthcare ecosystem [7]. Multi-agent systems enable distributed intelligence across heterogeneous healthcare networks by allowing agents to learn from changing contexts [8]. Nevertheless, traditional frameworks rely on centralized training, which introduces the risks of congestion and loss of exposures [9]. It is possible that the multi-agent learning can be embedded into a hierarchical control framework to enable localised anomaly suppression and global policy refinement or convergence. Such a concept is of paramount importance, particularly in latency-constrained applications as remote diagnostics and on-the-fly IoMT devices based on the continuous health monitoring of patients [10]. Furthermore, ensuring transparency and explainability of such learning processes has become a clinical demand and is an obligatory aspect in terms of medical data protection [11]. As such, a hierarchical learning ecosystem architecture including explainable deep reinforcement learning at both the edge and cloud layers can offer an additional antifragile cybersecurity defense in depth [12]. Recent works advocate hybrid cloud–edge deployment architecture in healthcare to reduce data flooding, increase data throughput and preserve privacy for distributed learning [13]. But despite these advances in technology, the telehealth systems are still facing challenges such as data sovereignty, reducing latency and flexible policy synchronizations between agents [14]. Privacy techniques activated at the edge (e.g., anonymization and differential learning) may bear positive potential of preserving patient data [15], however, these methods don’t seem to be highly elastic in such a way when used over heterogeneous network infrastructure hindering the response time [16]. With the shift in complexity of healthcare workloads there is an unprecedented requirement to adopt automated analytics systems that continuously harness high performance computing to focus on prioritizing important security threats [17]. These discrepancies can be reconciled using a hierarchical reinforcement learning approach, while real time decision making is performed by the edge agents, which have been implemented to operate as cloud coordinators and are still able optimize long term policies with experience sharing aggregation [18]. It considers this dis- tributed yet coordinated setup to find the right balance between privacy protection, flexibility, and agility in telemedicine cybersecurity [19]. Cyber Security and telemedicine – Not just a technical problem, but an ethical duty for patient confidence, medical reliability and digital health evolution. Although classical DL-based ID models are often accurate, they are mainly black boxes that lack clinical interpretability and regulatory approval [20]. We integrate explainable reasoning and policy distillation components into our hierarchical multi-agent architecture, which as a result makes it possible for the system to exchange justifications of security decisions in order to obtain transparency in respect automated reactions to security threats. Furthermore, by using slim agents all over edge devices, latency-sensitive functionalities (e.g., anomaly filtering and intrusion flagging) can be performed in real time without sending all events to the cloud. On the other hand, a central coordinator can collect up policies and optimize decision rules to achieve better long term survival. Such a two-layer
segments.label: human

segments.text: orchestration can make telemedicine cybersecurity as a self-learning, privacy-preserving and latency sensitive ecosystem. To realize this, the present work develops a Hierarchical Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning (HIER-MA-DRL) model that enables cloud–edge intelligence and possesses explainability and privacy protection properties to enhance cybersecurity of next-generation telemedicine systems. The main contributions of this paper are: ●​ H-MAC: Hierarchical Multi-Agent Coordination Our hybrid DRL framework offloads the computational cost of optimal multi-agent coordination in hierarchical structure from edge agents to a central coordinator by taking advantage of local (short-term) threat mitigation responses and global (longterm), OPTimal security learning. ●​ XPD Mechanism: We use the explainable reinforcement learning to transform complicated policy updates into readable decision-rational in reasoning processes, making it more transparent and reliable of telemedicine cybersecurity system response. ●​ Cloud–Edge Integration Combined with Privacy-Preservation & Latency-Optimisation: Incorporates device-side anonymization and federated learning to trade-off between confidentiality of patient data in face of real-time intrusion response, versus scalability being maintained against a backdrop of large-scale medical data. Organization of the paper: In Section II, we surveyed some related works focusing on privacy preservation, hierarchical intelligence, and DRL-based cybersecurity models in the telemedicine infrastructure. The proposed HIER-MA-DRL methodology is described in section III with its hierarchical agent architecture, policy, and explainable distillation. We detail the experimental design, dataset selection, performance metrics, and training parameters to validate detection accuracy and latency reduction in Section IV. The results and analysis, in Section V, compares the performance metrics such as detection rate, false positives, and computational latency of the proposed approach with centralized DRL frameworks. Section VI ends the paper with the main points and implications of the research and challenges for adaptive and privacy-aware cybersecurity in telemedicine. II Related Works Odeh et al. The detection accuracy of nearly 99% with 98% privacy protection, indicated the efficacy of this hybrid in enabling a scalable privacy-preserved approach to anomaly management in healthcare data streams. 2.1 Research Gap While much progress has been made through heterogeneous frameworks and computing paradigms throughout IoT, cloud and edge-enabled healthcare systems [1]–[17], there still remain substantial gaps in the privacy-preserving, detection accuracy and response latency

segments.text: triad. Existing solutions either tackle the problem in a centralized architecture that provides a high learning ability which comes with a high communication overhead and high latency in decisions [2], [3], or based on an edge lightweight framework that leads to a low detection accuracy due to light-weighting computations [5], [8]. While blockchain based [12] and multi-agent models [15] have provided significant improvements over existing systems in transparency and decentralization, at high volumes of telemedicine data streams they also introduce additional synchronization latency and scalability issues. Likewise, hybrid deep learning and reinforcement learning methods [9], [10], [17] demonstrate the potential for adaptive threat detection but also fail to incorporate hierarchical coordination mechanisms to ensure alignment of local edge solutions to global policies at the cloud-level. Additionally, in the context of DRL-driven cybersecurity explainability and interpretability have not been well studied, which not only hinders the trust of decision makers, but also regulatory conformance of medical environments [11]. One that combines edge-level responsive agent, cloud-level policy updating agent and privacy-preserving computing into a comprehensive hierarchical multi-agent DRL framework is thus required to deliver on-time, explainable and scalable cybersecurity for next-generation telemedicine infrastructures. III Proposed Methodology The HIER-MA-DRL approach in the proposed methodology exploits a hierarchical structure of three operational tiers—edge, and fog, and cloud—to realize adaptive privacy-preserved cyber-security in telemedicine environments [20]. At the edge tier, lightweight DRL (Deep Reinforcement Learning) agents conduct continuous device behaviour monitoring, also performing on-device anonymization, to safeguard patient data before it is transmitted. Fog layer serves as an interface to aggregate local threat intelligence and enable coordination between different agents in order to avoid alerts duplication and temporal consistency in responses [21]. At the same time, the cloud coordinator performs long-horizon policy optimization via deep Q-networks and actor–critic models, allowing for global knowledge and adjustment of local agent policies. To ensure that training can be distributed yet still efficient without compromising data privacy, we incorporate federate learning mechanisms into our method to allow training without revealing any raw data to make the model robust without sacrificing confidentiality. Privacy-preserving encryption, adaptive trust scoring, and edge offloading together enable a secure and efficient solution for telehealth environments [22]. Simulation environments mimic real telehealth traffic and agents are trained and evaluated on benchmark datasets for intrusion detection over multiple performance metrics such as accuracy, false positive rate, and response latency. Such an orchestrated multi-layered architecture will ensure the intelligence at local and global policies are consistent, making it further adaptable, scalable, and interpretable for real-time healthcare cybersecurity [23].

segments.text: Figure 1. Overall System Architecture of the Proposed HIER-MA-DRL Telemedicine Cybersecurity Framework The hierarchical operation of edge agents, the federated learning synchronization layer, and cloud-level DRL coordinator (for global policy optimization) are shown in Figure 1. The model updates get aggregated upward (in encrypted form) while the distilled policies and trusted refined trust scores are propagated back to the edge nodes for real-time adjustment to the anomalous nature of the traffic. With integrated cloud–edge stacks, it guarantees low-latency detection, data-processing with privacy-preservation and consistently high-performance on cyber-security in telemedicine environments. 3.1 Dataset Selection In this study, we used ToN_IoT dataset from the University of New South Wales (UNSW) since it reflects the realistic heterogeneous nature of Internet of Things (IoT) and edge network scenarios [24]. It successfully represents the network event behavior, including normal and malicious behavior in devices, gateways, application servers, which reflects a typical telemedicine architecture. ToN_IoT provides a greater diversity of telemetry data, OS logs, and network flow records than traditional intrusion detection datasets like NSL-KDD and CICIDS2018, which is especially important for emulating dynamic, distributed healthcare infrastructures. A broad spectrum of attack instances like distributed denial- of-service (DDoS), ransomware and data stealing available in the dataset allow for comprehensive testing of adaptive and multi-agent cyber defense maneuvers. Furthermore, this benchmark is an open-source dataset with appropriate annotation as well as simulates realistic IoT behaviour in real-time, hence a suitable option for testing privacy-preserved low-latency detection frameworks for telemedicine environment.

segments.text: 3.2 Dataset Description ToN_IoT dataset consist of multiple real-world benchmarks composed by network traffic data, IoT/IIoT telemetry and OS logs recorded under normal operations and attack simulations, mimicking realistic cyber–physical scenarios [25]. The dataset used in this study is shown include network and telemetry subset which consist of 2,500,000 labelled records with 46 extracted features per entry. Such features include IP addresses of source and destination, port numbers, protocol types, byte count, flow duration, packet rates, and readings from telemetry sensors. The dataset was preprocessed, which involves steps such as removing duplicates, dealing with missing values, normalization of numerical features, and anonymization to maintain privacy as much as possible, for further analysis. The extracted dataset was randomly split into three parts: 70% (1,750,000 samples) for training to optimise the multi-agent models, 15% (375,000 samples) for validation to tune the hyperparameters, and 15% (375,000 samples) for testing to assess performance repeatability and generalisability. This split ensured a variety of threat behaviors present during training whilst keeping the evaluation phase clear of bias. The ToN_IoT dataset offered the great class diversity, granularity, and comparatively balanced structure, making it a very effective and robust source for performing implementation and validating the proposed hierarchical multi-agent deep reinforcement learning framework of telemedicine cybersecurity. 3.3 Data Preprocessing Data integrity, consistency and privacy compliance control was achieved during the preprocessing phase before feeding the input into the hierarchical multi-agent deep reinforcement learning framework. Patient personal information sent between IoT, edge, and cloud nodes is anonymized and encrypted with homomorphic encryption, preventing the inference of an identity in both the learning and inference phases [34][36]. This is demonstrated by its continuous superiority in Figures 4–9, because the combination of hierarchical coordination, lightweight edge intelligence, and global policy optimization can keep the system highly responsive under dynamic telemedicine traffic requests. Both small accuracy spectrum, slowly in latency rise with more devices, and convergence stats imply that the framework is quite good even under heavy stress. Furthermore, the ablation study demonstrates that each of architectural parts matters for overall resilience on the system level as well, and which is a evidence of the wholistic design in proposed model. Collectively, our findings indicate that HIER-MA-DRL is a potentially rewarding and scalable cybersecurity defense in real-time privacy-sensitive telemedicine environment. VI Conclusion In conclusion, the paper proposed A Hierarchical Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning Framework (HIER-MA-DRL) for Low-Latency, Privacy-Preserving Cybersecurity for Cloud Based Telemedicine Systems with Machine Learning Applications The proposed model achieved better performance in all major metrics compared to five state-of-the-art approaches by means of edge-cloud integrated intelligence, adaptive threat detection, and explainable policy improvement. Through experimental results, the findings show promising detection accuracy of 99.03%, average response latency of 139.6 ms and false positive rate only 3.68%, which is practical for real-time clinical application. As for dynamic traffic, the framework showed a good scalability, as well as convergence stability. In upcoming studies an enhancement of the architecture will be performed by inserting quantum-assisted decision, optimization, coupling and cross-regional telemedicine networks, which will help gain more resilience and interoperability.
